text: The Moon is breaking up with us. Slowly.
Every year, it drifts three point eight centimetres further away. About as fast as your fingernails grow.
sub: Every year, it drifts 3.8 cm further away. About as fast as your fingernails grow.
asr: Every year it drifts 3.8 cm further away, about as fast as your fingernails grow.

text: We know because astronauts left mirrors up there. We still bounce lasers off them.
And honestly? It's our fault. Earth spins faster than the Moon circles us, so the ocean bulge it pulls on gets dragged ahead,
and that bulge tugs the Moon forward, flinging it a little higher every orbit.
The Moon pulls back, too. It's putting the brakes on Earth's spin.
When the Moon was young, it was so close it looked more than ten times bigger in the sky, and a day lasted less than ten hours.
sub: When the Moon was young, it was so close it looked more than 10 times bigger in the sky, and a day lasted less than 10 hours.
asr: When the Moon was young, it was so close it looked more than 10 times bigger in the sky, and a day lasted less than 10 hours.

text: When dinosaurs were around, a day was twenty-three and a half hours, and a year had three hundred and seventy-two of them.
sub: When dinosaurs were around, a day was 23.5 hours, and a year had 372 of them.
asr: When dinosaurs were around, a day was 23 and a half hours, and a year had 372 of them.

text: In about six hundred million years, it'll look too small to cover the Sun. No more total eclipses.
sub: In about 600 million years, it'll look too small to cover the Sun. No more total eclipses.
asr: In about 600 million years, it'll look too small to cover the Sun. No more total eclipses.

text: But it will never fully leave. The Sun will grow old and swallow the whole drama first.
So enjoy the eclipses. You live in the short time when the Moon fits the Sun perfectly.
